turns.text: If we take Support Vector Machines apart, which idea truly changed the direction of research?
In the early 1990s, machine learning needed methods that could generalize from limited data with clear mathematical guarantees. SVMs translated VC-style capacity control into a practical classifier.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?

SVMs prefer a boundary that is not merely correct on training data, but comfortably separated from the closest examples. Kernels make nonlinear boundaries possible while preserving a convex optimization problem.

Experts generally treat SVMs as mature classical methods whose conceptual importance exceeds their role in most modern deep-learning pipelines. Their long-term legacy is the margin-and-kernel view of generalization, robust boundaries, and nonlinear classification.
Seen alongside Ridge, Support Vector Machines reveals how the same technical question can echo across different eras.
